Stage 3 · Grammar

Defining relative clauses

What to say when you cannot remember the word.

Read the three clues from the warm-up, and two lines from today’s recording.
  • It’s something that you see in the street.
  • It’s something that birds sit on.
  • He’s the man who lives next door.
  • The house where we’re staying is huge.
  • One thing which I don’t like — they have no proper cooker.
What do these five words do?
Which word for which noun
The noun is…UseExample
a personwho  or  thatShe’s the woman who owns the house. · the friend that lent me the keys
a thing or animalwhich  or  thatIt’s a machine which washes the dishes. · something that birds sit on
a placewhereThe house where we’re staying is huge.
you don’t know the wordIt’s something that… · It’s someone who… · It’s a place where…
tense inside recycledthe machine which washes the dishes (usually) · the house where we’re staying (right now)
How to build one
  • Start with the general word: something / someone / a place / a thing
  • Add who / which / that / where
  • Finish with what it does, or what you do with it
  • It’s something + that + you dry yourself with → a towel
Two things to watch
  • Do not repeat the noun: the man who he lives next door
  • that covers people and things — it is the safe choice
  • where is for places only, never for things
  • With a thing you can drop the word: the bowl (that) you wash your hands in

WHAT THEY DO. A defining relative clause tells you which one. Without it the noun is not identified.

WHICH WORD. who for people, which for things, where for places, that for people or things.

WHY IT MATTERS. This is what you use when the exact word will not come. Describe it instead.

Not “the man who he lives here”, not “the machine where washes the dishes”.

In Lesson 6 these clauses come back inside directions.

WHAT THEY DO. A defining relative clause identifies the noun in front of it. Compare the man with the man who lives next door: the clause tells your listener which man you mean. Because the information is essential, there is no comma before it.

WHICH WORD TO USE. who for people, which for things and animals, where for places. that can replace both who and which, and in speech it is the most common choice of all — if you hesitate, use that. What you cannot do is use where for a thing: the machine which washes the dishes, never the machine where.

WORD ORDER. The relative word takes the place of the subject or object, so you do not repeat it: the man who lives here, not the man who he lives here. This is the single most common mistake with this structure.

LEAVING IT OUT. When the relative word is the object of the clause, English often drops it entirely: the bowl (that) you wash your hands in · the thing (which) I bought yesterday. When it is the subject you must keep it: the machine which washes the dishes.

WHY THIS LESSON EXISTS. Every learner forgets words. Instead of stopping, you describe: It’s something that you sleep under · It’s someone who cleans the streets · It’s a place where you hang your clothes. Three words — something, someone, a place — plus a relative clause will get you out of almost any gap.

The three to watch: “the man who he lives here” · “the machine where washes the dishes” · “the house which we’re staying” (needs where).

Both present tenses from Lesson 4 sit inside these clauses. In Lesson 6 you will use them to describe landmarks while giving directions.

From the coursebook recordings. Navigate B1 · Audio 2.4 and 2.6

Full grammar reference — Defining relative clauses

Form

A personthe man who cleans our street · (that is also possible)
A thing or animalthe shop which sells bread · (that is also possible)
A placethe street where I grew up
Possessionthe woman whose car was stolen
PositionThe relative word comes straight after the noun it describes.

When and why we use it

  • A defining clause says which person or thing you mean. Without it the sentence is not clear.
  • There are no commas around a defining clause.
  • Never repeat the subject: the man who he lives next door.
  • If the relative word is the object, you can leave it out: the book (which) I read last week.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • the woman which sells flowers → the woman who sells flowersWho for people.
  • the shop who sells bread → the shop which sells breadWhich or that for things.
  • the house where I live in → the house where I liveWhere already contains in.
  • the man who he lives here → the man who lives hereOne subject only.

Don’t confuse it with

Where replaces in which for places. Use which for the thing itself: the building which is opposite the bank.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

A house where the writer cannot name anything.

Before you read: the writer is looking after a stranger’s house for a month.

What do you think will be hardest about it?

A prediction, not an answer.

The house where I’m staying

I’m house-sitting for a friend of a friend this month. I’ve never met the owners — they’re the people who put an advert on a house-swap website, and I answered it.

The house is beautiful and completely strange to me. In the kitchen there’s a machine which washes the dishes, but I can’t find the button that starts it. There’s no proper cooker either, only the box that heats food in two minutes. I love cooking, so that is the thing which disappoints me most.

The bathroom is the room where everything confuses me. The bowl you wash your hands in looks like a sheet of paper, and on the first morning I couldn’t work the metal thing the water comes out of. There are candles everywhere, and towels so soft that I am almost afraid to use them.

In the bedroom there is nowhere to put my clothes — no tall cupboard where you hang things, and no low one with drawers either. There are white rugs on every floor, which is a problem for someone who spills things.

Outside, on the wall, there’s a big round dish that points at the sky, and a small camera which watches the front door. My friend says the owners collect old maps, and that the frames in the hall are worth more than my car. I am being very careful.

I’m enjoying it. But I still miss my own bed, my own duvet, and a kitchen where I know what everything is called.

Source note. Written for this course. The situation and the objects come from the house-sitting accounts in the Navigate B1 Unit 2 recordings.

You use it to…  You find it in the…  It’s made of…

Never say the word itself. Three clues, then let your partner guess.
